en: The Karṇa Parva (The Book of Karna)
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jaya).
When Droṇa had been slain at Kurukṣetra, Saṃjaya returned once more and reported to the king the wondrous battle between Karṇa and Pārtha.
Then Duryodhana, delighted by the words of the son of Droṇa, made Karṇa— the hero whose heart was filled with resolve— the leader of the armies.
Consecrated with jars made of jewels, that treasury of glory became the showerer of the nectar of desires for the king of the Kurus.
Having formed the Makara array, he stood amidst the enemy ranks;
the Pāṇḍavas, unwearied, formed the Ardhacandra array in response.
Then, as that terrible battle commenced, filled with sparks from the clashing of weapons and missiles, there arose a tumultuous roar free from all impurity.
Then Bhīma, mounted upon an elephant, slew in battle the fierce King of Kulūta, who was seated on a rutting elephant with four tusks.
Then, pierced by arrows released from the tip of Karna’s ear-like bow and shot from his bowstring,
the elephants fell like mountains whose wings had been severed.
Pārtha, Sātyaki, the Pāñcālas, the sons of Draupadī, and Śikhaṇḍin engaged with Kṛpa,
the son of Droṇa, and the others, making it appear as if a new day had begun.
Having slain the Saṃśaptakas, Pārtha led away the two kings,
Daṇḍadhāra and Daṇḍa, along with the city of Daṇḍadhārapura by means of his arrows.
Then Pāṇḍya, rending the army of the Kurus,
struck down the heads of the attacking kings with broad-headed arrows, having attained his mark.
Through policy, he constantly endures the rivalry between Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and Arjuna— which arises from the fever of pride— considering himself superior in strength.
She was tormented by his arrows— he who was the lord of the southern region, whose fame was the smile of a Karṇāṭī woman, and whose sharp weapons were the eyes of a Lāṭī woman.
Though restrained by the son of Droṇa, the son of the Sūta, the son of Subala, and Kṛpa,
the army of the Kuru king fled.
Approaching him with speed, the son of Droṇa, remaining unperturbed, fought that warrior who was raining down a shower of arrows like a thunderbolt, just as Indra fought Śambara.
Then the son of Droṇa severed with a broad-headed arrow the head of that lotus-like man, whose playful eyes were like bees and whose earrings were like bees hovering around it.
When the hero known as Pāṇḍya, the crest-jewel of kings, was slain,
the army of the Pāṇḍyas no longer shone, like a night deprived of the moon.

***** The Slaying of Pāṇḍya // 1 // ***** Then, as the heroes were deeply engaged in battle, drinking, as it were, the rain of weapons, and were possessed by pride, they fought without restraint. BhmJ 8.18.
When the chariots and elephants of the kings had become intermingled, and when the worlds were plunged into darkness by the thick dust that covered their bodies, Bhmj_8.19.
Nakula slew the Mleccha king Mahānīka, a fierce warrior who acted like a Rākṣasa and was skilled in all weapons.
In that dense crush, Karna, whose valor was rooted in truth, did not slay Akula— who had come within his range for slaughter— recollecting the words of Kunti.
Then the Pāñcālas and Sṛñjayas, overwhelmed by the heroes headed by Karṇa,
found no protection, nor did the Kurus find protection from Arjuna and his followers.

When the heroes had been slain and broken, when standards and chariots were shattered, and when the foot-soldiers were crushed by the masses of elephants whose trunks were deeply pierced and bleeding; ||| Bhmj_8.23 |||
In paths crowded with headless trunks whirled about in sudden, frantic dances, where elephants and horses were drowning in the vast rivers of blood; BhmJ_8.24 //
When the armies were exhausted and only the remnants remained, the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas,
their bows slackened, made for the withdrawal at the close of day.
***** The First Day of Battle // 2 // ***** Now, at dawn, when both armies were arrayed and drawn close together, Karṇa, surveying the Pāṇḍava host, spoke to Duryodhana: (Bhājana 8.26)
Having today become free from debt to my honor and my majesty, which were so dear through your grace, I shall go to rest in battle.
"Today, by slaying the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva— the very essence of your enemies—
I shall make fruitful this resolve of yours that has been cherished for so long."
In this world, the self-praise of one's own virtues is censurable in every respect by the virtuous;
however, they do not commend silence at times when action is required.
I am superior to Pārtha in both knowledge and prowess;
the only thing in which Kṛṣṇa is superior is that he possesses an invaluable charioteer.
"Śalya is known by all kings to be superior to Kṛṣṇa;
with him as my charioteer, I am confident that I can conquer Jiṣṇu."
When the son of Vikartana had spoken thus, King Suyodhana was delighted;
approaching him with humility, he addressed the King of Madra in that very manner.
Then the lord of Madra, enraged and with his garments disarrayed by his agitation, looked at the son of Rādhā with indignation and addressed the Kaurava king: Bhājya 8.33.
"O King, how great is your simplicity, which leads only to your own humiliation, since you have appointed me, who am so short in stature, to the office of charioteer! (Bhājana 8.34)
"Am I not capable of slaying all the Pāṇḍavas in battle? Why then do you wish to make me, a king, the charioteer of the Sūta's son? (Bhājana 8.35)
Having spoken thus, while Śalya was suddenly preparing to strike along with his followers,
the Lord of the Kurus appeased him and began to speak.
O King of Madra, you ought not to display such agitation at an improper time;
for you are indeed superior to Govinda, and therefore you are being requested by us here.
"Kṛṣṇa has been appointed by our enemies as a charioteer who is superior to Arjuna;
you are superior to Karṇa, therefore do not act with such obstinacy regarding the office of charioteer."

When the three worlds were overwhelmed by the Daityas— who had gained power through boons from Prajāpati and who dwelt in cities made of silver, iron, and gold according to their own will— (Bhagavadgītāmṛtavyākhyā 8.39).
In former times, when the worlds were being slaughtered, the gods, led by Śakra, went for refuge to the god Śaṅkara, the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Then, for the protection of the universe, the Lord of the Universe was entreated by the gods;
he fashioned a chariot composed of all the deities and made Viṣṇu his arrow.
Fully armored, he said to the gods, "Let a charioteer be appointed for me—
one whose power exceeds my own— by whom I may slay the Dānavas."
Then the gods, headed by Śakra, having deliberated for a very long time with their intellects,
appointed Brahmā, the creator of the universe, to the office of charioteer.
Then, when the chariot was seized by the goad of the syllable *Oṃ*, Hara consumed the Daityas,
who had become one with it, with the fire of his arrow.
***** The Narrative of the Destruction of Tripura // 3 // ***** Thus, in ancient times, even Dhātṛ himself became the charioteer of Rudra;
likewise, you too ought not to show contempt for Karna. Bhmj_8.45.
The virtuous indeed consider the fulfillment of a friend's request to be the true fruit of sovereignty, noble birth, virtues, and valor.
When Duryodhana had spoken thus, the King of Madra, with a smiling face, replied, "I am a charioteer who speaks according to his own will. (Bhājaka 8.47)
***** The Acceptance of Śalya as Charioteer ***** Then, as if with white horses fashioned by Mātali himself,
[Śalya] mounted Karna’s beautiful chariot, which was armored in refined gold. (Bhājana 8.48)
Śalya effortlessly grasped the well-trained reins,
just as the elder brother of Garuḍa [Aruṇa] holds the reins of the sun, the abode of splendor, in the sky.
Beholding Karṇa, the archer with Śalya as his charioteer, eager for battle,
the Kuru king along with his followers considered victory already within his grasp.
Amidst the sounds of conchs and kettledrums among the Kuru armies,
Karṇa, striking his bowstring, addressed the King of Madra.
Today, I suspect that upon seeing his son Arjuna slain by me, Śakra will in an instant cast a look of resentment toward my divine weapons.
Today, seeing Pārtha shattered by my arrows, let Yudhiṣṭhira suffer from the futility of his efforts to slay Bhīṣma and Droṇa.
To the son of Rādhā, Karṇa, who was speaking thus, the lord of Madra said:
"O Sūtaputra, do not utter such false prattle like a child."
Formerly, when you, though wise, had fled from the battle with the Gandharvas,
it was that hero of the three worlds who protected the Kauravas.
In that conflict over the seizure of cattle,
by him the silken garment was suddenly snatched away from those like you who were proud and had taken up their weapons.
O Karṇa, you who aspire to conquer him by whom Ākhaṇḍala, along with his followers, was defeated at Khāṇḍava— are you truly Karṇa, or are you not?
Thus repeatedly struck by Śalya as if by a dart, Rādheya suppressed his anger and addressed him, saying, "You shall see! (Bhājana 8.58)
Then, eager for battle amidst the arrayed divisions and ranks,
Karṇa, the foremost of preeminent chariot-warriors, questioned the soldiers.
Where is that hero, the enemy of Jayadratha, whose banner bears the monkey?
Without him, these arrows of mine languish in their impetuosity.
"To him who quickly brings Arjuna within the path of my vision,
I shall give variegated garments and ornaments."
Chariots, rutting elephants,
villages, and cities, as well as beloved women and various other riches, he gave him as much as he desired.
Having heard this, the King of Madra spoke with derision:
"O son of Rādhā, laughter arises from your own actions only to lead to sorrow."
Like a childless man on the verge of death regarding wealth accumulated over a long time,
why do you wish to abandon it to others out of delusion, without even reflecting?
You shall see Arjuna himself approaching, his white mane flowing,
like a timid deer before a lion with arrow-like claws.
Hearing this, Karṇa became enraged and, with a frowning face, said:
"You are devoid of virtue; you know neither me nor Dhanañjaya."
"I alone know Arjuna as a rival to the wielder of the Pināka bow, and he knows me in truth; you, however, boast falsely."
"This friend is actually an enemy; you have been sent to us by someone.
Or perhaps this crookedness is not surprising in one born of a wicked land."
The Madrakas are of contemptible conduct, devoid of truthfulness, virtue, and uprightness;
yet people who know all the Vedas proclaim pride to be their [highest] quality in this world. (Bhājana 8.69)
Shameless, wandering everywhere, and agitated by greed, delusion, and pride—
those ignoble women are both the sisters and the mothers of Madrikā.
Addressed thus with vehemence by the son of Rādhā, the lord of the Madras said:
"O fool, though much beneficial advice has been spoken, you do not understand."
"You are wise, yet your pride has vanished; you have been defeated by Savyasācin, and now, filled with remorse, you grieve over the words of beneficial advice."
In former times, there was a wealthy Vaiśya living on the shore of the ocean who had many children; protected by the king, he lived free from all affliction.
Among his sons was a crow who constantly fed on their leftovers;
he was well-nourished in body, a friend to the wealthy, and as dear to them as a son.
Then, once when some swans traveling from Lake Mānasa arrived, he spoke out of a sense of rivalry: "You are not my equals in speed."
"I know a full hundred ways of flying, distinguished by the techniques of gliding and soaring;
from this, your swiftness is known to be equal to mine."
Thus, by that eater of leftovers, the royal swans were provoked to leap about;
though called out to, those heroes within them merely smiled and said nothing at all.
But a single swan, with a smile upon his face, descended like an arrow from the sky along with the crow, having made an agreement with him that they would go together to the ocean.
By that wind-like speed, as the crow traveled through the sky level with the ocean,
within the distance of half a *krośa*, it became overwhelmed and its wings were broken.
Then, his pride shattered by that very [act], he was placed upon the shore by the compassionate one;
spitting blood, he regained consciousness after a long time, having learned of the other bird's end.
***** The Story of the Swan and the Crow ***** (5) // Just so, O Rādheya, surrounded by the Kauravas,
you too will become shorn of your pride upon encountering Arjuna in battle. Bhājana 8.81.
Having heard these words of the King of Madra, which were capable of piercing the vitals,
the heroic Vaikartana, though his anger was great, remained unperturbed and spoke.
"O Śalya, no fear arises in me from the words of those like you;
behold Arjuna struck down by me in battle! (Bhājana 8.83)

Long ago, my dear son, while practicing at the target, I pierced with an arrow a cow belonging to a brahmin who was performing a fire sacrifice, as he was hidden behind a thicket of trees. (Bhājana 8.84)
"Due to that curse, my chariot wheel will eventually reach its end;
this is my one vulnerability, for otherwise I am invincible."
But you, surrounded by this king and his army consisting solely of vehicles,
have yourself brought that double-tongued and crooked serpent into close proximity.
What can be said of you who are the ruler of the Madrakas—those of evil conduct, inhabitants of a sinful land, and devoid of the practices of the sacred fords? (Bhājana 8.87)
Those Madras who are your kinsmen constantly eat what is unfit for consumption, drink what is undrinkable, and take pleasure with women who should not be approached.
Women are common to all; the twice-born may eat anything;
and the Madras, among whom you are king, O monarch, are tainted by every kind of sin. (Bhājana-mālā 8.89)
***** The mockery of the Madras // 6 // ***** When Karṇa had spoken thus, the King of the Madras also replied:
"O Karṇa, you are the king of the Aṅgas, those who are guilty of abandoning their maternal uncle. BhmJ 8.90.
"In that realm where wives and sons are constantly sold by men, you should not speak thus to me, O Leader."
***** The Censure of His Limbs // 7 // ***** When the King of Madra had spoken thus, those horses, urged on,
rose up as if they had grown wings, tearing the earth asunder. Bhmj_8.92.
Then Jishnu, with his white horses and Achyuta as his charioteer,
was seen at the head of all the armies, intent on the destruction of the enemies.
Then, as the life-taking battle of heroes commenced,
the sound of twanging bows was drowned out by the resonance of musical instruments.
Śalya said to the son of Rādhā, who was eager for battle with Dhanañjaya:
"Behold the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, piercing the Kuru army! (Bhājaka 8.95)
Afflicted by hundreds of volleys of Pārtha’s arrows, these Saṃśaptakas remain hidden within the huts formed by the heaps of slain elephant herds.
Behold, O Arjuna, the pearl necklaces fallen from the throats of the kings, severed by your arrows,
appearing like garlands of tears shed by their royal fortunes.
When the lord of the Madras had spoken thus, the king said, "Where will Dhanañjaya go, having come within the range of my arrows out of joy? (Bhājana 8.98)
Then, when the interior of the world was filled with the arrows of Vaikartana,
the Pandava army trembled like a great forest in the wind.
Repeatedly depriving the heroes headed by Dhṛṣṭadyumna of their chariots,
Karṇa slew ten thousand warriors in an instant.
When the armies of the Cedis, Magadhas, and Pañcālas had been broken, Yudhiṣṭhira,
followed by great chariot-warriors, himself rushed toward the son of Rādhā.
"O favorite of the king, this is no verbal battle in which you excel," having said this, the son of Dharma covered Karṇa with arrows.
Then Karṇa, having slain the two great chariot-warriors who were the king's wheel-protectors with his arrows, crushed their banner and cut down their bows.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he hurled at Sūtavṛtra a sharp-pointed spear, fierce like the fang of Death, which emitted a thunderous roar.
Having shattered that bell-ringing spear,
Vaikartana cut through the king’s golden armor with his arrows.
Having overwhelmed him for a moment with swift arrows and shattered his armor, he struck down his horses,
which were ivory-colored with black manes.
Seeing the son of Dharma fleeing, the enraged Vṛkodara turned Karṇa back with arrows as fierce as thunderbolts.
Bhīma dispatched with his massive arrows the heroic younger brothers of Duryodhana, who had arrived by their brother’s command, to the abode of the city of the departed.
Nanda and Upananda, Durdharṣa, Mahābhuja the bow-wielder, Jarāsaṃdha, Śrutarvāṇ, and Durdina with his quiver.
Having slain the wrathful one with the noose in hand, clad in armor and possessing mighty arms,
he entered the army and crushed the division of elephants.
Then, in that slaughter of great warriors, Sātyaki, the Pāñcālas, the sons of Mādrī, and Yudhiṣṭhira fought against those led by Karṇa.
While the ocean of the army was being pierced by heroes led by Vṛṣasena,
the fierce sound of the Gāṇḍīva bow arose, striking against the very heavens.
When Dhanañjaya returned after having slain all the Saṃśaptakas,
the Kuru army suddenly turned back like a dancing whirlpool.
When the circle of kings headed by Suśarman had been broken by the weapons of the sons of Pṛthā,
Karṇa displayed the sport of Death among the Pandava armies.
Having slain seven tens of thousands of powerful lordly elephants,
he likewise brought about the destruction of an equal number of chariots belonging to the kings.
Vyāghraketu, Jaya, Śaṅku, Rudra, Ugrāyudha the supreme, Siṃhasena, Rocamāna, Śukta, Citrāyudha, and Hari. Bhmj 8.116.
Having slain Devāpi, Jiṣṇukarman, Śalabha, Citra, Daṇḍaka,
and other kings, he wrought a slaughter among the Pāñcālas.
Then, as it was being slaughtered by Karṇa and torn asunder in a thousand ways,
a new and terrible carnage occurred among the Pāṇḍava army.
By Karṇa, by the son of Droṇa, by Kṛpa, by Kṛtavarman,
by Kirīṭin, by the son of Pṛṣata, by the grandson of Śini, and by Śikhaṇḍin.
And by the enraged Bhīma, those two armies were split apart;
they became scattered, with their armor and weapons shattered.
Having conquered the son of Droṇa, who was raining down divine weapons, with his own divine weapon,
Phalguna beheld the great car-warriors being struck down by Karṇa.
The Lord of Madhu, amazed by Karna’s prowess, said to him:
"Behold, O son of Kuntī, this army consumed by the fire of Karna’s weapons. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.122)
Behold how the son of the charioteer was marked by the side-glance of Death;
for when he looked at me with a sidelong glance, he was already puffed up with pride in his role as a driver.
In an instant, the king makes that entire army sewn together;
behold, the quarters of the sky are covered by his dense net of arrows.
Having spoken thus, Keśava quickly led the son of Śakra by means of his thundering chariot to the vicinity of Bhīmasena’s chariot.
Then, having meditated upon Dharmarāja with a voice trembling with fear, Dhanañjaya [beheld him] proceeding slowly toward the camp, pierced by Karna’s arrows.
Sighing deeply and intensely tormented like a lion struck by a palm-strike,
he set out with the enemy of Kāliya to see his brother.
He saw the son of Dharma lying there, his armor shattered by arrows marked with Karna’s name and fletched with golden feathers.
Having saluted his feet, Keśava and Arjuna sat down;
with their bodies tormented by anxiety, they remained there for a moment, agitated.
Yudhiṣṭhira, perceiving that Karṇa had been slain and [the messenger] had arrived,
rose up without distress, filled with joy at his victory and with no small wonder.
O Pārtha, by good fortune Karna has been struck down by you in battle— he by whose fire of weapons our armies were for the most part utterly consumed.
"He was a hero, the slayer of his enemies, the leader of all archers, and the disciple of Rāma; tell me, how was that son of Vaikartana killed by you?"
Thus questioned by the king, Śvetavāhana replied:
"While he was fighting for a very long time with the son of Droṇa, who possessed the splendor of Rudra..."
And there was an obstacle for me in the felling of Karṇa caused by the Saṃśaptakas,
while the mighty-armed Bhīmasena remained stationed at the front of the opposing army.
"O Lord, I have come to see you wounded by blows;
now, permitted by you, [I shall go] to the refuge of the Kauravas."
"Even this hand of mine shall leave nothing remaining of Karṇa with arrows drawn back to his ear," said Bibhatsu;
and Kṛṣṇa, pained by the frustration of his resolve, [replied].
Covered with arrows and consumed by anger, the archer Yudhiṣṭhira,
having placed his immense burden upon Bhīmasena, spoke.
"You have fled from Karṇa after witnessing his prowess;
it was in vain that you were carried in Kuntī’s womb, bearing the marks of a kṣatriya."
Like a straw arrow in the count of sons, you were merely a filler;
those thirteen years were ordained for you as mere mental constructs.
All have gone to futility, like favors bestowed upon a base person;
who indeed could have known that Dhanañjaya was afraid of Karṇa?
"He who conducts himself according to this method shall emerge from the battle alive;
give this Gāṇḍīva bow to someone else who is endowed with valor."
"Who will remove from us the terror of Karṇa in battle?
Upon hearing this, Bībhatsu felt as if he had been struck in his very vitals.
At these words, he became enraged and cast tearful glances at his sword;
he was trapped in a terrible crisis of anger and within a continuous fire of suffering.
Seeing him fallen, Govinda, the all-pervading one, addressed him:
"O Pārtha, I know what is in your heart, because of which you waver repeatedly."
"O you of noble conduct, give the Gāṇḍīva to someone else; he who speaks thus to you is certainly to be slain by you—this is your well-known vow. (Bhājana 8.145)
Is it for that purpose that you, blinded by anger, seek to slay your elder brother,
or do you gaze at your sword out of fear of violating your vow?
Listen to this: you are utterly deluded by mere truth alone;
though firm in your vow of truth, you do not distinguish between dharma and adharma.
The unreal attains the nature of reality, while the real attains the nature of unreality;
this occurs at times through the differentiation of karma—thus it should be investigated by the wise with their intellect.
Even the Dharma is profound and subtle; it is not understood as it truly is.
Long ago, there was a hunter named Balāka in the forest.
Once, having suddenly slain a fierce beast that was destroying herds of cattle and groups of Brahmins with a single arrow, he attained the world of Śakra.
A Brahmin named Kauśika, who had previously observed the vow of truthful speech,
was asked by bandits where the fleeing creditors had gone.
That speaker of truth showed them those who were the refuge of virtue and compassion;
yet, having seen them, the bandits quickly slew them out of a desire for their wealth.
Then, in the course of time, Kauśika also fell and went to hell.
Thus, O Pārtha, the operation of truth and dharma is profound.
Therefore, toward your elder brother, King Yudhiṣṭhira, who is steadfast in righteousness,
you ought not to harbor any improper thought out of delusion.
Having heard this, Kṛṣṇa spoke again to Pārtha, who, pierced by the violation of his vow, had drawn his sword and was intent on killing himself.
By showing disrespect, one destroys the teacher in every way;
and by boasting in the assembly of teachers, one destroys oneself.
Protecting your vow and casting aside the ignorance born of anger, therefore,
O Phalguna, turn back now from this slaughter.
When the descendant of Daśārha had spoken thus, Dhanañjaya replied, "So be it," and then said to Yudhiṣṭhira, "You are a coward, a negligent man, and a cruel one."
"By me alone have all the Daityas and Dānavas been slain together;
I am the foremost among those who wield the bow," he said to himself. (Bhājana 8.159)
Then Hari, grasping the feet of Dharmasuta as he was prepared to depart for the forest out of grief, earnestly sought to appease him.
And Yudhiṣṭhira, his flood of resentment melting away, firmly embraced Pārtha as he lay prostrate at his feet with tearful eyes, holding him fast.
Then, having performed their purificatory rites, the two heroes, Dharmarāja and Dhanañjaya,
mounted their chariots, donned their armor, and proceeded to the field of battle.
Then, for a moment, that earth seemed to consist entirely of headless trunks due to the lords of men whose faces had been severed by the volleys of Arjuna’s arrows as they fell.
In the meantime, Bhīmasena, having slain the younger brothers of Duryodhana,
encountered Duḥśāsana as he was fighting with heroic prowess.
Having crushed his chariot, along with its horses, weapons, and banner, with his mace,
the husband of Hiḍimbā forcibly dragged that ruined man away in battle.
Then Vṛkodara, remembering the terrible humiliation of his beloved and possessed by the Rākṣasa of fury, drank warm blood.
Seeing that terrible deed of Bhīma, all the great chariot-warriors, their swords and bows fallen from their grasp, trembled in terror with their eyes closed.

Proud of the flow of blood, his face and cheeks bristling with horripilation, utterly unrestrained by intoxication and stumbling in his steps, the Son of the Wind shone with a terrifyingly radiant mace whirled in a fearsome frenzy; yet his mind remained intent on binding the hair of his beloved.
When Duḥśāsana was slain in that manner by means of an unprecedented method,
even the bodies of the greatest beings became bristling with thrill.
***** The Slaying of Duḥśāsana ***** // 8 // In the meantime, as the army of the Pāṇḍavas was being afflicted by the arrows of Vṛṣasena,
there arose a tumultuous roar from the falling elephants and horses. Bhājya 8.170.
Even when united, the kings protected by Bhīma and Sātyaki could not endure the blazing prowess of Karṇa’s son in battle.
He fought equally with Sātyaki, Bhīmasena, the two sons of Mādrī, Kirīṭin, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and other kings and heroes.
As that warrior fought with wonder, Arjuna, as if smiling,
severed his arms and his head, which resembled a lotus and its stalk.
***** The Slaying of Vṛṣasena // 9 // ***** When Vṛṣasena had been slain by the wielder of the *Gāṇḍīva* bow before him, Karṇa,
with tears in his eyes, remembered the son of Subhadrā who had been killed by many. Bhājaka 8.174.
Then, being consumed by the fire of wrath— with the fuel of indignation, the smoke-bannered comet of his furrowed brow— Karna rushed toward Dhanañjaya.
As the battle between the two proceeded, practiced through hundreds of past desires,
the sky became crowded with gods and siddhas who had come out of curiosity.
During that battle between Karṇa and Arjuna, when a dispute suddenly arose in the sky between the Sun and the Lord of the Gods, each of whom was proclaiming the victory of his own son.
In the past, when questioned by the gods who were divided into two factions, Śiva and Brahmā declared with certainty: "Where Kṛṣṇa is, there victory lies. (Bhājana-mālā 8.178)
Then Śauri and Śalya blew their deep-sounding conchs, Karṇakarṇin and Kirīṭin, by which the three worlds trembled.
Then the son of Vikartana dispatched a flight of arrows toward the Pāṇḍava— arrows whose white tips seemed marked by his own fame.
Struck by the banner of Pārtha, Karṇa’s standard trembled;
and a third part of Kṛṣṇa’s gaze pierced Śalya like a barb.
Then, as the quarters were continuously filled with Arjuna’s arrows,
the Kaurava soldiers stood at a distance beyond the range of his shafts.
Then the one whose banner bears the ape carried away the faces of the great chariot-warriors who were protecting the chariot of Radheya, as they had been dispatched by Duryodhana.
Then, remaining unperturbed, Karṇa repeatedly cut down the mass of arrows being discharged at the base of Kirīṭin’s fist.
Then Bhīma spoke to Pārtha, and Acyuta was greatly amazed:
"Karna is difficult to defeat in battle; stand firm and fight, O Phalguna! (Bhājana 8.185)
O hero, take up a fury even greater than that which you displayed at Kairāta, at Khāṇḍava, or even during the slaughter of the Kālakeyas.
Hearing this, Vijaya, his bracelets jingling as he moved,
drew the Gāṇḍīva bow tightly and filled the heavens with divine weapons.
Having neutralized that shower of weapons with the Bhārgava missile, Karṇa covered Kirīṭin,
Bhīma, and Kṛṣṇa with his arrows.
Then, due to the showers of Karṇa’s arrows and Arjuna’s weapons on all sides,
a vast destruction occurred among the armies of both the Pāṇḍus and the Kauravas.
Then Karṇa discharged at Savyasācin a blazing serpent-faced weapon, adorned with sandalwood paste and possessing a great hood.
Once that serpent had been released, Śalya said to the Lord of Aṅga:
"This serpent sent by you will not reach the throat of Pārtha."
Furthermore, O Rādheya, you are capable of reconciliation if you so desire;
or rather, you have always been deaf to words beneficial to Karṇa.
Thus addressed by Śalya for the purpose of diminishing his prowess, the son of Tapaṇa—the pure-hearted Karṇa—replied: "Karṇa does not strike twice."
Seeing the most terrible serpent, fierce with venom, falling from his ear as it approached, Hari assumed a body as massive as Mount Mandara.
When the four horses had then descended to the earth upon their knees,
the serpent seized the tip of the crown of the diadem-wearing Arjuna as he bowed down.
When the fragment of the crown, laughing with its pearls and gems, fell,
that serpent, deceived and hissing, entered the earth.
Then Karna, laughing repeatedly, pierced Krishna and Arjuna with arrows resembling the staff of Death, which he released from his ear-drawn bow and shouted aloud.
Then the son of Śakra, out of anger, cut through Karṇa’s armor adorned with divine jewels and filled his body with arrows.
Having cut with six arrows that great serpent who had harbored enmity toward him at Khāṇḍava and was now ascending into the sky, Pārtha struck Karṇa once again.
When the Brahmā weapon had been neutralized by the son of Vaikartana, Arjuna manifested the Śakra weapon to destroy it,
which was filled with hundreds of thunderbolts and lightning strikes.
Having destroyed that weapon, Rādheya severed the bowstring of Kirīṭin;
in an instant, Dhanañjaya fitted a new string to his bow.
Then Arjuna discharged a fierce weapon, its mass of flickering flames blazing forth,
by which the sky became terrifying with a dreadful conflagration of the quarters.
In the meantime, by the power of destiny, at that very moment in the battle with the King of Aṅga, the Earth herself seized the chariot wheel.
Then Karna, standing in a precarious position and intent on lifting that wheel, said to the son of Kuntī: "May you wait for a moment."
"Now that this discus has been withdrawn by me, release your great weapon, O Phalguna!
For heroes such as you do not strike one who is in distress and disarmed."
Having heard this, the slayer of Kāliya laughed and said to Karṇa:
"By good fortune, O Karṇa, you now understand dharma, remaining steadfast in the vow of a hero."
Have you forgotten how the foolish son of Subhadrā was slain by many?
And let that which you said to Kṛṣṇā in the assembly hall be counted as well.
"You have been remembered as one whose righteousness was severed by the administration of poison and fire;
surely, in times of calamity, the conduct of base kings is devoid of dharma."
When Janārdana had spoken thus, Vijaya, as if blazing with fury,
neutralized with a Brahma-missile the Brahma-missile that Karṇa had discharged.
Having neutralized the *āgneya* weapon discharged by Arjuna with his own *vāruṇa* weapon, the lord of Aṅga remained suspended with his chariot-wheel devoured.
Then the son of Akhaṇḍala struck Karna’s banner, which was radiant with gold and as lofty as his own desire, with an arrow.
Then, having taken up an arrow adorned with gold in the añjali-gesture,
he consecrated it with mantras and drew it back, its tip as black as the fangs of Death.
"If Rudra and the other masters of weapons are pleased with my asceticism,
then by means of this [missile] I shall slay the enemy," having said this, Arjuna released it.
Suddenly pierced in the throat, which was adorned with a necklace,
the son of Rādhā fell like a golden palm tree cut down by a saw.
When Karṇa, the foremost of archers and the leader of the Kaurava army, was slain,
Śalya quickly went toward him, piercing the hearts and faces [of his enemies] like thorns.
Seeing the lord of the Madras arrived in an empty chariot, the kings exclaimed, "Duryodhana has been slain, but Karṇa lives! (Bhājana 8.216)
When the King of Aṅga had been struck down by Arjuna’s arrows, Duryodhana,
his senses overwhelmed, was as if unconscious, like a severed head.
Then, a radiance emerged from the body of Karṇa, whose rays were flickering, and entered the orb of the sun;
by this, the sky for a moment became matted with masses of flames, while the celestial chariots crumbled away into space.
Thus ends the Karṇaparvan in the Bhāratamañjarī composed by Kṣemendra.
